info.bio:
Bad Religion es una banda de Punk Rock estadounidense fundada en 1980 en el sur de California por Greg Graffin (voz), Jay Bentley (bajo), Jay Ziskrout (batería) y Brett Gurewitz (guitarra). La banda ha contado con diferentes alineaciones a lo largo de sus muchos  años de existencia, siendo Graffin el único miembro que ha sido constante; no obstante la banda cuenta hoy en día con 3 de sus miembros originales.

Son conocidos comúnmente por haber

scenes.name: Hardcore
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El punk como «violento, rápido y ruidoso» tarda en conquistar EE UU, pero cuando lo hace el hardcore se convierte durante dos décadas en el idioma nacional de millones de chavales. Misfits y el «scum-rock»; el crossover punk-metal (Suicidal Tendencies, Corrosion Of Conformity, Agnostic Front); Mission Of Burma en Boston. Washington: Bad Brains (reggae, funk y metal diez años por delante), Minor Threat (el «straight-edge») y Rites Of Spring, inventores del emo-core. San Francisco: Dead Kennedys de Jello Biafra, D.R.I. (thrash antes que Metallica), Flipper. Los «beach punks» de Los Ángeles: Germs, X, Black Flag (Damaged), Descendents, Gun Club (Fire Of Love), Bad Religion. El jazz-core de Minutemen y Saccharine Trust; en el Medio Oeste, Husker Du y Replacements cambian el hardcore para siempre; en Chicago, Naked Raygun y Big Black de Steve Albini; en Europa, The Ex y los italianos CCCP.
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

podcast.title: Founding of Epitaph Records (1980)
podcast.body: Bad Religion founded their own independent label, Epitaph Records, in 1980, creating a significant platform for punk and indie music. "the band that founded their own label, Epitaph Records, in 1980"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation of Epitaph Records (1981)
podcast.body: Due to the lack of distribution for their self-produced records, Bad Religion formed their own independent label, Epitaph, in 1981. This label would go on to become a significant force in the indie punk scene. "And that's when the group formed an indie label called Epitaph in 1981."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Label Release (Late 1993)
podcast.body: In late 1993, after years of releasing music independently through their own label, the band was persuaded to release their next album on Atlantic Records, a major label that was part of Warner. "In late 1993, the band that founded their own label, Epitaph Records, in 1980, were themselves persuaded to release their next album on a major, Atlantic Records, who were part of Warner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Discography by 1994
podcast.body: By 1994, Bad Religion had already released seven albums and numerous singles, demonstrating a prolific career prior to the mid-90s punk explosion. "By the time 1994 rolled around, they had released seven albums and a ton of singles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 924 Gilman Street Alumni
podcast.body: Bad Religion are counted among the alumni of 924 Gilman Street, the significant all-ages punk club in West Berkeley, California. Because of the club's stringent policy against major label bands, Bad Religion is no longer permitted to perform at the venue. "Gilman Street alumni like Green Day and the offspring and AFI and Primus and even bad religion aren't really welcome anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Shrines ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Academic Writings Available Online
podcast.body: For those interested in his scholarly work, Greg Graffin's academic writings can be accessed through links provided on the Bad Religion website. "If you would like to read some of his academic writings, there are links on the Bad Religion website."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Accused of Blasphemy and Sacrilege
podcast.body: When Bad Religion left their indie imprint, Epitaph, for a major record label, punk purists condemned the decision as "blasphemy and sacrilege." This reaction highlighted the ideological clash between punk's DIY ethos and mainstream commercialism. "And bad religion, with a major record label leaving their own indie imprint, epitaph, behind, blasphemy and sacrilege."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ancient Bird Species
podcast.body: Greg Graffin of Bad Religion has an ancient bird named after him, *Kyliania Grafini*, which lived in China approximately 120 million years ago. This honor is particularly significant for Graffin, who is also a paleontologist. "Greg Graffin of Bad Religion has Kyliania Grafini, which is a bird that lived in China about 120 million years ago."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Formation
podcast.body: Bad Religion formed in 1980 when a group of high school students, inspired by early hardcore bands like Black Flag, the Circle Jerks, and The Germs, decided to participate in the scene. "They came together in 1980 when a bunch of high school students, inspired by the likes of Black Flag, the Circle Jerks, and the germs, decided that they wanted a piece of the action."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Booking by Kevin Lyman
podcast.body: Kevin Lyman, the future founder of the Warped Tour, booked Bad Religion for performances at California State Polytechnic University in Pomona when they were just starting out in the early 1980s. "What he would basically do is hire bands like Bad Religion and the Bangles when those groups were just starting out in the book at the university."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Distribution Struggles
podcast.body: Bad Religion, a Southern California punk band, faced similar challenges as Black Flag in the early 1980s, unable to find anyone willing to distribute their self-produced records. This led the band to take a do-it-yourself approach to ensure their music reached an audience. "They also couldn't find anyone willing to distribute their self-produced records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enduring Career
podcast.body: Established in 1979, Bad Religion experienced a peak in 1994-95 but continues to tour and release new music to this day. "Bad Religion, established 1979, peaked 1994-95 and still touring and still making records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Epitaph Records Founders
podcast.body: The band founded Epitaph Records, which became one of the most important independent labels of the era, showcasing their commitment to the DIY ethic. "Their label, Epitaph, was one of the most important indie labels of the era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Epitaph Records Legacy
podcast.body: After self-releasing their debut, Epitaph Records evolved into one of the most significant independent labels globally, famously taking a chance on The Offspring, which led to their success. "Now Epitaph, of course, would later become one of the most important indie labels in the entire world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation and Inspiration
podcast.body: Bad Religion formed in 1980, founded by a group of high school students who were inspired by established hardcore bands like Black Flag, The Circle Jerks, and The Germs, and wanted to contribute to the emerging hardcore movement. "They came together in 1980, when a bunch of high school students, inspired by the likes of Black Flag, the Circle Jerks, and the germs, decided that they wanted a piece of the reaction."

podcast.title: Founding Epitaph Label
podcast.body: Bad Religion, like Black Flag, faced the challenge of no one wanting to release their music. This compelled them to establish their own label, Epitaph, which initially served as a platform solely for their own records but later grew significantly beyond hardcore punk. "Another band that found themselves in the same boat as Black Flag was Bad Religion. No one wanted to release their stuff either, so they had to establish their own label, and they called theirs Epitaph."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: Funding Epitaph Records
podcast.body: The band Bad Religion funded Epitaph Records, a punk rock label based in Orange County, California. Like Merge Records, Epitaph was founded by a band seeking an alternative to the major label system, and it eventually achieved massive success with The Offspring. "Epitaph was funded by a band that was unsatisfied with the major label system. In this case, the group was Bad Religion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Greg Graffin's Extensive Academic Career
podcast.body: Greg Graffin embarked on an impressive academic journey, double-majoring in anthropology and geology at UCLA before earning a master's degree in geology. He then pursued and obtained a PhD in Zoology from Cornell University. His doctoral thesis, titled "Monism, atheism, and the naturalist worldview, perspectives from evolutionary biology," explored the links between evolutionary biology, history, and the philosophy of science. "Greg enrolled in UCLA where he double majored in anthropology and geology."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hardcore Legends with DIY Ethos
podcast.body: Bad Religion established themselves as legends within the hardcore community, particularly recognized for their strong DIY (Do It Yourself) approach to creating and distributing their records. "They'd become legends with the hardcore crowd, especially with their DIY attitude towards making and releasing records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hardcore with Pop Sensibilities
podcast.body: Bad Religion possessed impeccable hardcore credentials, known for their strong political, socially aware, and rage-fueled lyrical content. However, they distinguished themselves by integrating a "smooth edge" through melodic vocals and harmonies, effectively applying "pop sensibilities" within their hardcore sound. "impeccable hardcore credentials, lots of politics, social awareness, and rage. But at the same time, they gave everything a smooth edge with melodic vocals and even harmonies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Harvard Secular Society Award
podcast.body: In April 2008, Greg Graffin received an "outstanding Lifetime Achievement Award and Cultural Humanism" from the Harvard Secular Society, recognizing his contributions and respected standing in academic and humanist circles. "in April of 2008, he received an outstanding Lifetime Achievement Award and Cultural Humanism from the Harvard Secular Society."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Pacific Northwest Rock
podcast.body: Bad Religion was mentioned as a hardcore punk band from California that influenced the rock environment of the Pacific Northwest, which was crucial for the unmolested development of grunge. "bands like the dead Kennedys and black flag and bad religion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rehab at Impact Drug and Alcohol Treatment Center
podcast.body: Brent Gerowicz of Bad Religion attended the Impact Drug and Alcohol Treatment Center in Pasadena, where he notoriously had drugs smuggled into him inside hollowed-out fruit. "He, by the way, used to have more drugs smuggled into him inside the rehab center that were inside hollowed out fruit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Spreading Hardcore Gospel
podcast.body: Bad Religion, alongside Black Flag, was instrumental in disseminating the "gospel of hardcore" through their consistent touring efforts. "And there were bands like Black Flag and Bad Religion that spread the gospel of hardcore by touring constantly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Teaching Life Sciences at UCLA
podcast.body: When he is not performing or recording with Bad Religion, Greg Graffin dedicates his time to teaching life sciences at UCLA, maintaining an active role in academia. "When Greg isn't working with bad religion, he's teaching life sciences at UCLA."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tony Hawk Video Game Feature
podcast.body: Music from Bad Religion was featured in Tony Hawk's popular skateboarding video games. "Tony Hawk's video games sold by the millions, and each one featured appropriate music from groups like The Vandals and Laguewagon, Suicidal tendencies, Millen-Call and Bad Religion, and so many more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Transition to Major Label
podcast.body: Bad Religion, initially working on their independent label Epitaph Records, was eventually convinced to sign a major record deal. This move sparked considerable controversy among punk purists. "They had been working on their own independent epitaph records, and they were convinced to sign a major record deal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Warped Tour Feature
podcast.body: Bad Religion was among the bands that performed during the early years of the Warped Tour, a significant platform for pop punk and ska punk acts. "In just the first few years, the tour featured bad religion."

xref.title: Anthony Kiedis's "Last Chance" Rehab (1997)
xref.body: A trip to India sparked a spiritual awakening for Anthony Kiedis. Upon returning to Los Angeles in 1997, he checked into a "last chance" rehab place called the Impact Drug and Alcohol Treatment Center in Pasadena for about a month, a facility known for hosting members of Mötley Crüe and Brent Gerowicz of Bad Religion. This visit initially seemed successful. "A trip to India put him in a spiritual place, and when he got back to LA, he checked into a last chance rehab place called the Impact Drug and Alcohol Treatment Center in Pasadena for about a month."

xref.title: Band Origins and Label Strategy
xref.body: Rancid evolved from the revered band Operation Ivy and were label-mates with Bad Religion on Epitaph. Their songs were known for being short, tight, and melodic, perfectly complementing the sound kids sought after Green Day's success. They balanced punk ethics with commercial reach by remaining on Epitaph while securing distribution and quiet promotion from Warner Brothers. "Not only was Ransett label-mates with bad religion, but they devolved out of a band called Operation Ivy, a group that was revered by a young Billy Joe Armstrong, who of course was in Green Day"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: California Hardcore Scene
xref.body: The Offspring were deeply rooted in the California hardcore scene, a fierce but small community dedicated to punk that evolved from the original 1970s punk. This music became a soundtrack for skaters and snowboarders, including bands like Dead Kennedys, The Adolescents, The Vandals, Black Flag, and Bad Religion, which was niche and rarely played on radio. "Everyone was into California hardcore. The punk that evolved out of the original punk of the 1970s. The scene was small but fierce and its adherents stuck together. And some of this music became the soundtrack for skaters and snowboarders, dead candidates, the adolescence, the vandals, black flag, bad religion, really niche stuff at the time, and certainly stuff that never made it on the radio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Commitment to Indie Label
xref.body: Unlike Green Day, Rancid opted to remain an independent band, recording their music for Epitaph Records, the label founded by members of Bad Religion. "But unlike Green Day, Ranset chose to stay indie, recording for Bad Religion's Epitaph Records."

xref.title: Founding Alternative Tentacles
xref.body: The Dead Kennedys formed Alternative Tentacles, a California label, initially just to release one of their singles. They enjoyed the experience so much they decided to turn it into a full-time business, following the model of Black Flag with SST and Bad Religion with Epitaph. The label also played a key role in exporting American hardcore by developing relationships with other indie labels worldwide. "At first, they just wanted to get one of their singles out there, but they enjoyed the experience so much that they decided to turn Alternative Tentacles into a full-time business..."

xref.body: Dela Roka started playing guitar at the age of eight. xref.body: Black Flag was noted for spreading the "gospel of hardcore" through constant touring. Their music was also part of the "unique stew of influences" that shaped the Seattle sound, where it was not considered strange to be into both hardcore punk and traditional hard rock simultaneously. "And there were bands like Black Flag and Bad Religion that spread the gospel of hardcore by touring constantly. ...No one considered it weird to be into both Black Flag and Arasmith at the same time."
